steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on out-of-distribution detection for Transformers, where the method (BLOOD) looks at how smoothly representations are transformed between layers. Motivate the problem, explain why the prerequisites of OOD methods matter in practice, describe the method and evaluation briefly, and finish with a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- What OOD detection is
- DNN-based OOD detection and the problem of prerequisites
- Grouping OOD methods by prerequisites: black-box, white-box, open-box
- Our method: BLOOD for Transformers, and how we evaluate it
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- What OOD detection is
  - ML models assume evaluation data comes from same distribution as training data = in-distribution (ID)
  - real-world deployment: noisy, imperfect -> data from a different distribution = OOD; hurts performance
  - telling ID from OOD apart = OOD detection (cite survey)
- DNN-based OOD detection and prerequisites
  - DNNs: consistent SOTA across diverse ML tasks (cite) -> lots of attention in OOD research
  - popular baselines: posterior class probabilities (cite); but DNN overconfidence (cite) erodes their credibility
  - alternative: representation learning; similar instances encoded close together -> distance of OOD instance to training-set representations (cite)
  - downside: need training data at prediction time or intervene in training
  - practical problem: third-party models pre-trained on non-public data now standard; e.g. Hugging Face Transformers library (cite) - community models, little detail on training
- Three categories by prerequisites
  - obvious fix: methods with minimal prerequisites
  - research largely ignores differing prerequisites; comparisons treat them equally, ignore practical applicability
  - (1) Black-box: only input-output mappings; models integrated into a product
  - (2) White-box: access to weights + knowledge of architecture; fits third-party pre-trained models
  - (3) Open-box: unrestricted access to model and training resources; training interventions, training data, separate OOD train/validation sets
- Our method: BLOOD
  - focus: Transformer architecture (cite), predominant in many ML domains
  - exploits differences in how Transformers process ID vs OOD data; white-box, broad practical applicability
  - Between Layer Out-Of-Distribution (BLOOD) Detection: smoothness of between-layer transformations of intermediate representations; smoother for ID than OOD
  - evaluated on Transformer-based pre-trained LLMs, text classification (most prevalent NLP task)
  - beats other SOTA white-box methods and even some open-box ones
  - analysis of why ID/OOD are transformed differently; two other shifts: semantic and background
  - code and data provided
- Contributions
  - (1) BLOOD: works with only model weights (third-party pre-trained models, de facto standard); smoothness = square of Frobenius norm of Jacobian; unbiased estimator for computational limits
  - (2) experiments on Transformer LLMs for text classification: beats SOTA white-box methods; advantage bigger on complex datasets than simple ones; better on background shift than semantic shift
  - (3) analysis of source of the difference: learning algorithm focuses on changing ID region of representation space -> smooths ID transformations; OOD region mostly unchanged, except e.g. complex tasks where it is changed and sharpened

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Machine learning (ML) models work well under the assumption that they will be tested on data from the same distribution as the data they were trained on, which is called the in-distribution (ID) data. But when models are deployed in the real world, which is noisy and imperfect, they often get data from a different distribution, the out-of-distribution (OOD) data, and this can hurt the models' performance. Telling apart ID and OOD data is usually called OOD detection.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have consistently reached state-of-the-art performance on many different ML tasks, so they have gotten a lot of attention in OOD detection research. Popular baselines use the posterior class probabilities of the model, but DNNs are often overconfident and this makes these probabilities less credible. Another group of methods uses the fundamental concept of DNNs, which is representation learning. A DNN encodes similar instances close to each other in its representation space, so an OOD instance can be found from the distance between its representation and the representations of other instances in the training set. The problem with these methods is that they need the training data to be there at prediction time or they need to intervene in the training of the model. This is a big practical limitation, because using third-party models that were pre-trained on non-public data is more and more the standard practice. For example, the Hugging Face Transformers library provides community models but often does not give full details about how they were trained.

- Three categories by prerequisites
  - obvious fix: methods with minimal prerequisites
  - research largely ignores differing prerequisites; comparisons treat them equally, ignore practical applicability
  - (1) Black-box: only input-output mappings; models integrated into a product
  - (2) White-box: access to weights + knowledge of architecture; fits third-party pre-trained models
  - (3) Open-box: unrestricted access to model and training resources; training interventions, training data, separate OOD train/validation sets

- Our method: BLOOD
  - focus: Transformer architecture (cite), predominant in many ML domains
  - exploits differences in how Transformers process ID vs OOD data; white-box, broad practical applicability
  - Between Layer Out-Of-Distribution (BLOOD) Detection: smoothness of between-layer transformations of intermediate representations; smoother for ID than OOD
  - evaluated on Transformer-based pre-trained LLMs, text classification (most prevalent NLP task)
  - beats other SOTA white-box methods and even some open-box ones
  - analysis of why ID/OOD are transformed differently; two other shifts: semantic and background
  - code and data provided

- Contributions
  - (1) BLOOD: works with only model weights (third-party pre-trained models, de facto standard); smoothness = square of Frobenius norm of Jacobian; unbiased estimator for computational limits
  - (2) experiments on Transformer LLMs for text classification: beats SOTA white-box methods; advantage bigger on complex datasets than simple ones; better on background shift than semantic shift
  - (3) analysis of source of the difference: learning algorithm focuses on changing ID region of representation space -> smooths ID transformations; OOD region mostly unchanged, except e.g. complex tasks where it is changed and sharpened

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Machine learning (ML) models work well under the assumption that they will be tested on data from the same distribution as the data they were trained on, which is called the in-distribution (ID) data. But when models are deployed in the real world, which is noisy and imperfect, they often get data from a different distribution, the out-of-distribution (OOD) data, and this can hurt the models' performance. Telling apart ID and OOD data is usually called OOD detection.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have consistently reached state-of-the-art performance on many different ML tasks, so they have gotten a lot of attention in OOD detection research. Popular baselines use the posterior class probabilities of the model, but DNNs are often overconfident and this makes these probabilities less credible. Another group of methods uses the fundamental concept of DNNs, which is representation learning. A DNN encodes similar instances close to each other in its representation space, so an OOD instance can be found from the distance between its representation and the representations of other instances in the training set. The problem with these methods is that they need the training data to be there at prediction time or they need to intervene in the training of the model. This is a big practical limitation, because using third-party models that were pre-trained on non-public data is more and more the standard practice. For example, the Hugging Face Transformers library provides community models but often does not give full details about how they were trained.

An obvious way to close this resource gap is to use OOD detection methods that need as little as possible. However, current OOD detection research has mostly ignored that OOD detection methods have different prerequisites, and comparisons often treat methods with different prerequisites in the same way, without asking whether they are practically applicable. In practice it makes sense to put OOD detection methods into three categories: (1) Black-box, for methods that can work on black-box models (i.e., with access only to input-output mappings), so they are suitable for models integrated into a product; (2) White-box, for methods that need access to the model's weights and know its architecture, so they can be applied directly to third-party pre-trained models; and (3) Open-box, for methods that have unrestricted access to model and training resources, so they can intervene in the training process and/or use training data or separate OOD train or validation sets.

In this paper we focus on OOD detection for the Transformer architecture, which has become the main architecture in many ML domains. We introduce a new OOD detection method that uses the differences in how Transformers process ID and OOD data. The method is white-box and could be applied widely in practice. Our Between Layer Out-Of-Distribution (BLOOD) Detection method estimates how smooth the between-layer transformations of intermediate representations are, and it builds on the insight that these transformations are usually smoother for ID data than for OOD data. We evaluate BLOOD on Transformer-based pre-trained large language models used for text classification, which is the most common task in natural language processing (NLP), and we find that it does better than other state-of-the-art white-box OOD detection methods and even some open-box methods. We also analyze BLOOD to look into why ID and OOD intermediate representations are transformed differently, and we evaluate BLOOD on two other types of distribution shift, semantic shift and background shift. We provide code and data for our experiments.

Our contributions are: (1) We propose BLOOD, a new OOD detection method that can be used even when only the model's weights are available, e.g., with third-party pre-trained models, which are becoming the de facto standard in many fields. BLOOD uses information about how smooth the between-layer transformations of intermediate representations are. We measure this smoothness with the square of the Frobenius norm of the Jacobian matrix, and we give an unbiased estimator for it to deal with computational limitations. (2) Our experiments on Transformer-based pre-trained large language models for text classification show that BLOOD does better than other state-of-the-art white-box OOD detection methods. Our results also show that the advantage is bigger on complex datasets than on simpler ones. We also show that BLOOD detects background shift better than semantic shift. (3) Based on our main insight that between-layer transformations of ID data are smoother than those of OOD data, we analyze where this difference comes from. We find that the learning algorithm focuses more on changing the ID region of the intermediate representation space, and in doing so it smooths the between-layer transformations of ID data. The OOD region of the space is mostly left unchanged, except in some cases, e.g., for more complex tasks, where the OOD region is also changed and becomes sharper as a result.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Machine learning (ML) models' success depends on the assumption that the model will be evaluated on data coming from the same distribution as the data it was trained on, the in-distribution (ID) data. However, models deployed in noisy and imperfect real-world scenarios often face data from a different distribution, the out-of-distribution (OOD) data, which can hinder the models' performance. The task of distinguishing between ID and OOD data is commonly referred to as OOD detection [1].

Owing to their consistent state-of-the-art performance across diverse ML tasks [2], Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have received significant attention in OOD detection research. While popular baselines use the model's posterior class probabilities [3], the overconfidence of DNNs [4] often erodes the credibility of these probabilities. An alternative is offered by methods that leverage the fundamental concept of DNNs, namely representation learning. Because a DNN encodes similar instances close together in its representation space, an OOD instance can be identified from the distance between its representation and the representations of other instances in the training set [5]. The downside of these methods is that they require the training data to be present during prediction or involve intervening in the model's training procedure. This is a significant practical limitation, since using third-party models pre-trained on non-public data is increasingly the standard practice. A case in point is the Hugging Face Transformers library [6], which provides community models but often lacks comprehensive details about their training.

An obvious way to close the resource gap is to rely on OOD detection methods with minimal prerequisites. However, current OOD detection research has largely ignored the differing prerequisites of OOD detection methods, often leading to comparisons that treat methods with different prerequisites equally and disregard the question of practical applicability. From a practical perspective, it makes sense to group OOD detection methods into three categories: (1) Black-box, for methods that can operate on black-box models (i.e., with access only to input-output mappings) and are thus suitable for models integrated into a product; (2) White-box, for methods that require access to the model's weights and knowledge of its architecture, and are thus readily applicable to third-party pre-trained models; and (3) Open-box, for methods with unrestricted access to model and training resources, allowing interventions in the training process and/or access to training data or separate OOD train or validation sets.

In this paper, we focus on OOD detection for the Transformer architecture [8], which has become the predominant architecture in numerous ML domains. We introduce a novel OOD detection method that leverages the inherent differences in how Transformers process ID and OOD data. The method is white-box and has potential for broad practical applicability. More concretely, our Between Layer Out-Of-Distribution (BLOOD) Detection method estimates the smoothness of between-layer transformations of intermediate representations, building on the insight that these transformations tend to be smoother for ID data than for OOD data. We evaluate BLOOD on Transformer-based pre-trained large language models applied to text classification, the most prevalent task in natural language processing (NLP), and find that it outperforms other state-of-the-art white-box OOD detection methods and even some open-box methods. We further analyze BLOOD to probe the underlying causes of the differences in how ID and OOD intermediate representations are transformed, and we evaluate BLOOD on two other types of distribution shift -- semantic and background shift. We provide code and data for our experiments.

The contributions of this paper are as follows: (1) We propose BLOOD, a novel OOD detection method applicable even when only the model's weights are available, e.g., third-party pre-trained models, which are becoming the de facto standard in many fields. BLOOD uses information about the smoothness of the between-layer transformations of intermediate representations. We quantify this smoothness using the square of the Frobenius norm of the Jacobian matrix, for which we provide an unbiased estimator to alleviate computational limitations. (2) Our experiments on Transformer-based pre-trained large language models for text classification show that BLOOD outperforms other state-of-the-art white-box OOD detection methods. Additionally, our results indicate that the performance advantages are more prominent on complex datasets than on simpler ones. We also show that BLOOD is more effective at detecting background shift than semantic shift. (3) Following our main insight that between-layer representation transformations of ID data tend to be smoother than those of OOD data, we analyze the source of this difference. We find that the learning algorithm focuses more on changing the ID region of the intermediate representation space, smoothing the between-layer transformations of ID data in the process. At the same time, the OOD region of the intermediate representation space is largely left unchanged, except in some scenarios, e.g., for more complex tasks, when the OOD region is also changed and sharpened as a consequence.
